questions.q: What is the primary role of the first-person narrator in the essay "oqQVt"? Choose the best option: (A) To tell a fictional story about a house, (B) To argue a legal case about property rights, (C) To explore the cultural and philosophical meanings of 'home' through personal reflection, (D) To describe architectural features of traditional Indian houses.
questions.a: Correct answer: (C). The narrator uses personal memory, etymology, and Sanskrit texts to investigate what 'oqQVt' truly means beyond a physical structure. A wrong answer (A) reveals the student mistakes the essay for a short story. (B) shows confusion with expository/argumentative writing. (D) indicates focus on literal description rather than the narrator's reflective purpose.

questions.q: The author writes: ":i O;fDr&lR; gS] uke lekt&lR;A" (Form belongs to the individual; name belongs to society). Explain in your own words what this distinction reveals about the narrator's view of identity.
questions.a: The narrator believes true identity (:i) is an inner, individual reality, while names (uke) are external labels imposed by society, history, and tradition. He resists being defined solely by social categories (caste, profession, titles). A wrong answer that says "name is more important" or "both are the same" misses the narrator's core philosophical stance — he privileges the inner self over social designation, which is central to his persona as a thinker who questions convention.

questions.q: In the passage where the author describes his childhood courtyard (iwQy), well (Nk¡g), and neem tree, identify TWO literary devices used and explain how each helps build the narrator's persona as someone deeply rooted in tradition.
questions.a: 1. Sensory imagery (गंध, ध्वनि, स्पर्श) — e.g., "ड्योढी पर नीम की छाया", "कुएँ की जगत पर बैठे बच्चे" — creates visceral connection to place, showing the narrator as an embodied participant in tradition, not an abstract scholar. 2. Allusion to Sanskrit terms (oqQVt, oqQVuh, oqQfVgkfjdk) — demonstrates his scholarly persona, bridging lived experience and textual knowledge. A wrong answer listing only "description" or "metaphor" without linking to persona shows inability to connect device to character revelation.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's attitude toward "thuk" (renunciation) in the shloka "fHkÙok ik"kk.kfiBja..." with his attitude toward the courtyard (iwQy) as a space of "vijkftr LoHkko". What tension does this reveal in his persona?
questions.a: The narrator honors the *ideal* of renunciation (thuk) as a high spiritual path ("thuk Hkh ,d dyk gS... riL;k gS") but simultaneously celebrates the courtyard as a space of engaged, sensory, worldly belonging ("vijkftr LoHkko"). This reveals a persona that does not reject the world for spirituality, but seeks *integration* — the courtyard *is* his spiritual ground. A wrong answer saying "he prefers renunciation" or "he rejects spirituality" flattens his nuanced both/and perspective, missing the essay's central synthesis.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the author's strategy of blending personal anecdote (childhood well, neem tree) with etymological analysis (Sanskrit roots of oqQVt) to convey his concept of home. Is this blend persuasive? Why or why not?
questions.a: Yes, it is persuasive because the anecdotes ground the abstract etymology in lived emotion (memory, loss, belonging), while the etymology elevates the personal into cultural wisdom. The persona becomes both *grandson listening to grandmother's stories* and *scholar interpreting Sanskrit* — a dual authority that mirrors the essay's thesis: home is both intimate and universal. A wrong answer calling it "confusing" or "unnecessary" fails to see how the blend *enacts* the name/form unity the author argues for.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the narrator's perspective, set ten years after the essay's events, reflecting on whether the "oqQVt" of his childhood still exists for him. Use at least two phrases/concepts from the essay (e.g., iwQy, :i vs uke, thuk).
questions.a: A strong entry will show the narrator's continuing philosophical voice — perhaps noting the physical courtyard is gone (name/uke changed) but the *form* (:i) of belonging persists in memory and practice. It should reflect the tension between thuk (letting go) and vijkftr LoHkko (engaged belonging). A weak entry will be purely nostalgic ("I miss my house") without philosophical depth, revealing the student hasn't internalized the narrator's analytic persona.
